# Overview



Quantum-based refinement represents a significant advancement in structural biology, combining quantum chemical methods with crystallographic and cryo-EM data to improve biomolecular structure accuracy. Q|R (Quantum-based Refinement) is an open-source module that replaces traditional parameterized library-based restraints with chemically accurate restraints derived from quantum chemical calculations, offering superior accuracy especially for novel molecules like drugs or cofactors that lack comprehensive experimental parameterization.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L11)

## The Core Challenge

Biomacromolecular refinement using quantum chemistry faces a fundamental scaling challenge—quantum mechanical methods have computational complexity that scales poorly with system size. Traditional quantum chemistry approaches cannot handle the thousands of atoms typically found in proteins, nucleic acids, and other biological macromolecules within practical timeframes. This limitation has prevented widespread adoption of quantum-based restraints in structural refinement workflows, despite their theoretical advantages in accuracy and transferability to novel molecules.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L12-L18)

## The Fragmentation Solution

Q|R solves this scaling problem through an innovative divide-and-conquer fragmentation approach that breaks large biological systems into manageable pieces. Each fragment can be treated with quantum mechanical methods individually, then combined to provide complete system restraints. The system employs sophisticated clustering algorithms based on interaction densities to optimally partition molecules, ensuring that chemically relevant regions remain intact while maintaining computational tractability.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L19-L23), [fragmentation.py](fragmentation.py#L20-L28)

## System Architecture

The Q|R architecture follows a modular design with clear separation of concerns across computational, structural, and optimization components. The system orchestrates quantum mechanical calculations through a flexible calculator system that supports multiple quantum chemistry engines and machine learning potentials. Key architectural components include fragmentation managers that partition the system, restraints managers that compute energies and gradients, and an optimization engine that drives coordinate updates using conjugate gradient or ASE-based minimization algorithms.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph Input["Input Layer"]
        PDB[PDB Structure]
        MAP[Experimental Map]
        PARAM[User Parameters]
    end
    
    subgraph Core["Core Processing"]
        FM[Fragmentation Manager]
        QM[QM Engine Calculator]
        RM[Restraints Manager]
    end
    
    subgraph Optimization["Optimization Engine"]
        WG[Weight Calculator]
        MIN[Minimizer]
        CONV[Convergence Check]
    end
    
    subgraph Output["Output Layer"]
        RLOG[Results Log]
        RPDB[Refined PDB]
        MET[Metrics]
    end
    
    PDB --> FM
    MAP --> FM
    PARAM --> FM
    FM --> QM
    QM --> RM
    RM --> WG
    WG --> MIN
    MIN --> CONV
    CONV -->|not converged| RM
    CONV -->|converged| RLOG
    CONV --> RPDB
    CONV --> MET
```

Sources: [refine.py](refine.py#L1-L20), [driver.py](driver.py#L301-L310)

![Q|R Workflow](https://github.com/qrefine/qrefine/blob/master/doc/icons/QR1-2.png?raw=true)

## Core Components

The fragment manager handles system partitioning using interaction-based clustering algorithms, ensuring chemically meaningful fragment boundaries while maximizing computational efficiency. The calculator system provides a unified interface to multiple quantum chemistry backends, from traditional ab initio methods (Gaussian, ORCA, PySCF) to semi-empirical approaches (MOPAC, xTB) and modern machine learning potentials (AIMNet2, ANI, FairChem). The restraints manager coordinates energy and gradient calculations, seamlessly switching between quantum mechanical and standard CCTBX restraints based on user configuration and system requirements.

Sources: [refine.py](refine.py#L77-L81), [restraints.py](restraints.py#L48-L51), [restraints.py](restraints.py#L434-L452)

## Supported QM Engines

Q|R offers extensive compatibility with quantum chemical methods through a modular plugin architecture supporting over a dozen different calculation engines. Traditional quantum chemistry packages include Gaussian, ORCA, PySCF, Turbomole, and Terachem for high-accuracy calculations, while semi-empirical options like MOPAC and xTB provide faster approximations suitable for larger systems. The system also integrates cutting-edge machine learning potentials including AIMNet2, ANI, TensorMol, and FairChem, which offer near quantum-chemical accuracy at computational speeds approaching classical force fields.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L72-L77), [calculator.py](calculator.py#L1-L5)

> [!TIP]
> The AQuaRef implementation using AIMNet2 provides particularly efficient refinement, combining neural network potentials with quantum-based restraints for significantly accelerated calculations while maintaining chemical accuracy.

## Optimization and Weighting

The refinement engine implements adaptive weight factor calculation that automatically balances experimental data against restraints during optimization. The system monitors bond RMSD throughout refinement, dynamically adjusting restraint weights—doubling when bond RMSD is high to prioritize geometry, and halving when bond RMSD is low to better fit experimental data. This adaptive approach, combined with robust convergence criteria and multiple minimization algorithms (conjugate gradient and ASE-based optimizers), ensures stable convergence to chemically and physically meaningful structures.

Sources: [calculator.py](calculator.py#L1-L5), [calculator.py](calculator.py#L26-L27), [driver.py](driver.py#L22-L34)

## Project Structure

The Q|R codebase follows a clear modular organization with separation between user interfaces, core algorithms, quantum chemistry integrations, and testing infrastructure. The command-line interface provides accessible entry points for refinement, fragmentation, charge calculation, and testing workflows. Core modules handle fragmentation strategies, restraint computation, optimization driving, and result management. The plugin architecture encapsulates quantum chemistry engine specifics, while comprehensive test suites include unit tests for component validation and regression tests for system integrity.

```
qrefine/
├── command_line/    # CLI entry points (qr.refine, qr.fragment, qr.test)
├── Core modules     # refine.py, driver.py, restraints.py, calculator.py
├── plugin/ase/      # QM engine integrations (mopac_qr.py, gaussian_qr.py, aimnet2_qr.py)
├── tests/           # Unit tests, regression tests, acceptance tests
├── config/          # Environment specifications (conda, cuda, phenix)
└── examples/        # Example datasets and workflows
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L42-L58)

## Applications and Use Cases

Quantum refinement provides particular advantages for challenging structural biology scenarios. Low-resolution crystallographic data (beyond 3Å) benefits significantly from chemically accurate restraints when traditional library parameters may not capture true molecular geometry. Novel molecules including drug candidates, cofactors, ligands, and modified residues can be refined more accurately since quantum-based restraints don't rely on pre-existing parameterization. Cryo-EM structures also benefit from Q|R's real-space refinement capabilities, which directly optimize model fit to density maps using quantum mechanical restraints.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L10)

## Installation Options

Q|R provides multiple installation pathways tailored to different user needs and computational environments. CCTBX-only installation offers a fully open-source route suitable for developers and users comfortable managing conda environments. Phenix integration provides a fully automated, user-friendly experience recommended for most structural biologists, leveraging Phenix's extensive ecosystem and graphical interfaces. Docker containers offer reproducible environments for both development and production use, with images available for CUDA 11 and CUDA 12 configurations to support GPU-accelerated quantum chemistry calculations.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L24-L29), [README.md](README.md#L60-L61)

## Getting Started

The recommended learning path begins with understanding installation requirements and options. Users should review the [Quick Start](2-quick-start) guide for basic workflow familiarity, then proceed to installation instructions matching their environment: [Phenix Installation](3-phenix-installation) for most users, [CCTBX Installation](4-cctbx-installation) for developers, or [Docker Setup](5-docker-setup) for containerized deployments. After successful installation, the command-line option `qr.refine --show-defaults` displays all available parameters and default values for exploration.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L62-L67), [README.md](README.md#L69-L77)

## Next Steps

For users ready to begin working with Q|R, the recommended progression continues with practical workflow guidance. The [Quick Start](2-quick-start) page provides hands-on examples to run your first refinement, followed by [Understanding Fragmentation](7-understanding-fragmentation) to learn how the system partitions biomolecules. Those interested in specific quantum chemistry backends should explore the [Supported QM Engines Overview](11-supported-qm-engines-overview) to select appropriate methods for their research needs. Advanced users may proceed directly to [Quantum Refinement Concepts](6-quantum-refinement-concepts) for deeper theoretical understanding of the methodology.


# Quick Start



Welcome to Q|R (Quantum Refinement), a tool that combines quantum chemistry with crystallographic refinement to improve biomacromolecular structures, especially when working with low-resolution data from X-ray crystallography or cryo-EM experiments. This guide will get you running your first refinement in minutes.

![qrefine workflow](https://github.com/qrefine/qrefine/blob/master/doc/icons/QR1-2.png?raw=true)

## What You'll Learn

This Quick Start guide covers the essential steps to:
- Install Q|R using conda
- Verify your installation with built-in tests
- Prepare your structural model for refinement
- Run your first quantum refinement using MOPAC
- Understand the basic workflow and command-line options

After completing this guide, you'll be ready to explore more advanced features like [Understanding Fragmentation](7-understanding-fragmentation), different QM engines in [Supported QM Engines Overview](11-supported-qm-engines-overview), and the clustering algorithms in [Clustering Algorithms](9-clustering-algorithms).

## Installation

Q|R supports two installation paths. For beginners and researchers wanting the fastest path to productive refinement, the **CCTBX conda installation** is recommended.

### Prerequisites

Before installing Q|R, ensure you have:
- Python ≥ 3.9
- Conda binary (miniconda or mamba recommended)
- 2-5 GB of free disk space

### CCTBX Installation (Recommended for Open Source Users)

The CCTBX installation provides a complete open-source environment with MOPAC and xTB quantum engines pre-configured:

```bash
# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/qrefine/qrefine.git qrefine && cd qrefine

# Create conda environment with all dependencies
conda env create -n qrefine -f environment.yaml

# Activate the environment
conda activate qrefine

# Configure Q|R within CCTBX
bash ./build_into_conda.sh

# Source the paths (run this for every new shell)
source <path_shown_in_previous_step>/setpaths.sh
```

Sources: [environment.yaml](environment.yaml#L1-L22), [cctbx.md](cctbx.md#L1-L44)

### Alternative: Phenix Installation

If you're already a PHENIX user, Q|R integrates seamlessly with the PHENIX suite:

```bash
# Activate your PHENIX environment
source path_to_phenix/phenix_env.sh

# Navigate to qrefine and install
cd qrefine
sh build_into_phenix.sh
```

Sources: [phenix.md](phenix.md#L1-L33)

> [!TIP]
> For Apple Silicon users, clustering on macOS may be unreliable due to pair interaction issues. Use the alternative environment configuration: `conda env create -n qrefine -f config/arm64-osx.yaml`

## Verification: Run Built-in Tests

After installation, verify everything works correctly by running the test suite. This step is crucial—it confirms your environment is properly configured before you start working with your own data.

```bash
# Create a temporary directory for tests
mkdir test_qrefine && cd test_qrefine

# Run the test suite
qr.test
```

The test suite exercises core functionality including refinement, restraint calculations, and quantum engine integration. If all tests pass, your installation is ready for production use.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L39-L44), [command_line/test.py](command_line/test.py)

## Understanding the Q|R Workflow

Before diving into refinement commands, it's helpful to understand the Q|R architecture. The system divides large biomacromolecules into smaller, quantum-chemically tractable fragments using a **divide and conquer** approach:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Input PDB + MTZ] --> B[Model Preparation]
    B --> C{Restraints Type?}
    C -->|CCTBX| D[Standard Crystallographic Restraints]
    C -->|Quantum| E[Fragmentation & Clustering]
    E --> F[QM Energy Calculations]
    F --> G[Restraint Generation]
    D --> H[Refinement Engine]
    G --> H
    H --> I[Output: Refined PDB]
    
    style D fill:#e1f5ff
    style E fill:#fff4e1
    style F fill:#ffe1f5
```

The workflow consists of three main phases:

1. **Model Preparation**: Completing missing atoms, adding hydrogens, and validating structure
2. **Restraint Calculation**: Either using standard CCTBX restraints or generating quantum-derived restraints via fragmentation
3. **Refinement**: Optimizing atomic positions against experimental data using calculated restraints

Sources: [refine.py](refine.py#L1-L20), [README.md](README.md#L10-L20)

## Your First Refinement: CCTBX Mode

The fastest way to get started is using **CCTBX restraints**, which employs standard parameterized library-based restraints. This mode is ideal for initial refinement runs and for systems where quantum refinement isn't necessary.

### Basic Command Structure

The primary command for refinement is `qr.refine`, which requires:
1. An MTZ file containing experimental data (structure factors)
2. A PDB file containing the atomic model
3. Optional parameters to control refinement behavior

Sources: [command_line/qr.py](command_line/qr.py#L1-L9), [tests/unit/run_tests.py](tests/unit/run_tests.py#L49-L62)

### Running a CCTBX Refinement

Here's the simplest possible refinement command:

```bash
qr.refine your_structure.pdb your_data.mtz restraints=cctbx
```

This command will:
- Load the experimental data and structural model
- Use standard CCTBX restraints for geometric constraints
- Run optimization cycles to minimize the discrepancy between model and data
- Output a refined PDB file (typically named `your_structure_refined.pdb`)

**Example output**:
```
Rw: 0.3230 Rf: 0.3113 Rf-Rw: -0.0117 rmsd(b):  0.0151 rws:  1.000 n_fev: 0
...
Best r_work: 0.2526 r_free: 0.2966
```

Sources: [examples/3dtj/README.md](examples/3dtj/README.md#L43-L63)

### Available Command-Line Options

To see all available options and their default values:

```bash
qr.refine --show-defaults
```

Key parameters you might want to adjust:

| Parameter | Default | Description |
|-----------|---------|-------------|
| `restraints` | `cctbx` | Type of restraints: `cctbx` (fast) or `qm` (quantum) |
| `max_iterations_refine` | 100 | Maximum refinement cycles |
| `data_weight` | auto | Weight of experimental data vs. restraints |
| `clustering` | True | Enable/disable fragmentation (for large systems) |
| `output_folder_name` | None | Directory for output files |

Sources: [qr.py](qr.py#L12-L78), [README.md](README.md#L68-L72)

## Model Preparation: Adding Missing Atoms

Quantum refinement requires a **complete atomic model** with all hydrogen atoms and missing side-chain residues present. The `qr.finalise` tool automates this preparation step.

### Running Model Completion

```bash
qr.finalise your_structure.pdb
```

This command:
- Adds missing hydrogen atoms using Reduce/ReadySet
- Completes missing side-chain atoms and termini
- Validates the overall charge of the molecule
- Outputs `your_structure_complete.pdb`

**Example validation**:
```bash
# Check charge before finalisation (may show nonsensical results)
qr.charges your_structure.pdb verbose=true
# Output: Charge: -1292 (invalid)

# Check charge after finalisation
qr.charges your_structure_complete.pdb verbose=true
# Output: Charge: 0 (valid)
```

Sources: [command_line/finalise.py](command_line/finalise.py#L1-L116), [examples/3dtj/README.md](examples/3dtj/README.md#L99-L136)

> [!TIP]
> Always run `qr.finalise` before quantum refinement. Incomplete models can cause QM calculations to fail or produce meaningless results. The tool also checks that the total charge is physically reasonable.

## Quantum Refinement with MOPAC

Once you have a complete model, you can perform **quantum refinement** using the MOPAC semi-empirical QM engine. This provides more accurate chemical restraints than standard library-based methods.

### Basic Quantum Refinement Command

```bash
qr.refine your_complete.pdb your_data.mtz restraints=qm engine=mopac
```

This command triggers the full Q|R pipeline:
1. Fragments the structure into manageable pieces (default: ≤15 residues per cluster)
2. Computes QM energies and gradients for each fragment using MOPAC
3. Generates quantum-derived geometric restraints
4. Refines the structure using these restraints against experimental data

### Example from Test Data

Q|R includes test data you can use to practice:

```bash
# Navigate to test data directory
cd qrefine/tests/unit

# Run quantum refinement with MOPAC
qr.refine data_files/m00_poor.pdb data_files/2olx.mtz \
  restraints=qm engine=mopac clustering=False mode=opt
```

The `mode=opt` parameter performs geometry optimization without experimental data weighting, useful for testing QM calculations.

Sources: [tests/unit/tst_01.py](tests/unit/tst_01.py#L36-L45), [README.md](README.md#L74-L79)

## Clustering for Large Systems

For systems larger than ~500 atoms, Q|R automatically applies **clustering** to divide the structure into smaller fragments. You can inspect and control this process.

### Inspecting Cluster Configuration

```bash
qr.cluster your_structure.pdb
```

This displays:
- Maximum residues per cluster (default: 15)
- Residue indices assigned to each cluster
- Clustering time and statistics

**Example output**:
```
max number of residues in each cluster: 15

Residue indices for each cluster:
[[120, 121, 122, 123, 124, 125, 126, 127, 128, 129, 130, 131, 146],
 [189, 190, 192, 193, 194, 195, 196, 197, 198, 199, 200, 201, 202],
 ...]

Time: 53.6436
```

Sources: [examples/3dtj/README.md](examples/3dtj/README.md#L75-L94), [command_line/cluster.py](command_line/cluster.py#L1-L9)

### Visualizing Fragments

To understand how your structure is being fragmented for QM calculations:

```bash
qr.fragmentation your_complete.pdb
```

This generates PDB files for each fragment with buffer regions, allowing you to visually inspect the fragmentation strategy in molecular visualization tools like PyMOL or VMD.

**Output files created**:
- `0.pdb`, `1.pdb`, `2.pdb`, ... - Individual fragments
- `0_cluster.pdb`, `1_cluster.pdb`, ... - Fragments with buffer regions
- Point charge files for electrostatic embedding

Sources: [examples/3dtj/README.md](examples/3dtj/README.md#L148-L184), [command_line/fragmentation.py](command_line/fragmentation.py#L1-L52)

## Troubleshooting Common Issues

### Installation Fails

**Problem**: Conda environment creation fails
- **Solution**: Ensure you have conda ≥23.10 or use mamba for faster dependency resolution

**Problem**: Module not found errors after installation
- **Solution**: Make sure you've sourced the `setpaths.sh` script as shown in the installation section

### Refinement Errors

**Problem**: "No model file found"
- **Solution**: Check that you're providing both PDB and MTZ files in the correct order: `qr.refine model.pdb data.mtz`

**Problem**: QM calculations fail to converge
- **Solution**: Try `gradient_only=1` to use only QM gradients without full energy minimization: `qr.refine model.pdb data.mtz engine=mopac gradient_only=1`

**Problem**: Clustering takes too long
- **Solution**: Reduce `maxnum_residues_in_cluster` parameter: `qr.refine model.pdb data.mtz cluster.maxnum_residues_in_cluster=10`

### Test Failures

**Problem**: Unit tests fail during verification
- **Solution**: Always run tests in an empty directory. The tests create files and can conflict with existing data: `mkdir test_dir && cd test_dir && qr.test`

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L39-L44), [examples/3dtj/README.md](examples/3dtj/README.md#L30-L38)

## Project Structure Overview

Understanding the Q|R codebase organization helps when exploring advanced features:

```
qrefine/
├── command_line/       # Main entry points (qr.refine, qr.finalise, qr.cluster)
├── config/             # Configuration files for different QM engines
├── doc/                # Documentation and HTML files
├── examples/           # Tutorial examples (1us0, 3dtj, AQuaRef)
├── plugin/ase/         # QM engine interfaces (mopac, gaussian, orca, xtb, aimnet2)
├── tests/              # Unit tests and regression tests
├── qr.py              # Main refinement program with parameter definitions
├── refine.py          # Core refinement logic
├── fragmentation.py   # Fragmentation and clustering algorithms
└── restraints.py      # Restraint generation from QM calculations
```

Sources: [Repository structure](.), [qr.py](qr.py#L1-L100)

## Next Steps

Now that you've completed the Quick Start, you're ready to explore more advanced features:

1. **Learn about fragmentation strategies**: Understanding how Q|R divides structures is crucial for large systems. Read [Understanding Fragmentation](7-understanding-fragmentation) to learn about buffer regions, charge embedding, and different clustering algorithms.

2. **Explore quantum engines**: MOPAC is just one of many QM engines available. Discover faster alternatives like [AQuaRef and AIMNet2](17-aquaref-and-aimnet2) for GPU-accelerated refinement, or high-accuracy options in [Gaussian Integration](13-gaussian-integration) and [ORCA Integration](14-orca-integration).

3. **Master restraint systems**: Deepen your understanding of the differences between [QM vs CCTBX Restraints](20-qm-vs-cctbx-restraints) and how to manage complex restraint scenarios.

4. **Advanced optimization**: Learn about [Weight Factor Calculation](24-weight-factor-calculation) to balance experimental data against chemical restraints, and explore different [Minimization Algorithms](25-minimization-algorithms) for challenging refinement problems.

5. **Production workflows**: See how the examples directory applies these concepts to real structures. The 3dtj example demonstrates a complete workflow from model preparation through quantum refinement.

Remember to consult the [Overview](1-overview) for context on when quantum refinement is most beneficial—particularly for low-resolution data, novel ligands, or systems where standard restraints may be insufficient.

# Phenix Installation



This guide provides comprehensive instructions for installing Q|R (Quantum Refinement) into an existing Phenix installation. Q|R extends Phenix's refinement capabilities by integrating quantum chemical restraints, enabling more accurate structure refinement for biomolecules using quantum mechanical methods. The installation process supports both standard installer versions and developer source builds of Phenix, with options for GPU-accelerated AQuaRef components.

## Installation Overview

Before proceeding with Phenix installation, ensure you meet the following prerequisites:
- Python ≥ 3.9
- Existing Phenix installation (installer or source build)
- Conda binary (miniconda recommended)
- Appropriate system permissions (may require sudo)
- For GPU acceleration: NVIDIA GPU with CUDA support (optional)

The Phenix installation offers two primary approaches: **fully automated installation** (recommended for most users) and **semi-manual installation** (preferred for developers). Both methods detect your Phenix installation type automatically and configure Q|R accordingly.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Start Phenix Installation] --> B{Choose Installation Method}
    B -->|Most Users| C[Fully Automated]
    B -->|Developers| D[Semi-Manual]
    
    C --> E{Need GPU Support?}
    E -->|No| F[Run: sh build_into_phenix.sh]
    E -->|Yes CUDA 11| G[Run: sh build_into_phenix.sh aimnet2 cuda11]
    E -->|Yes CUDA 12| H[Run: sh build_into_phenix.sh aimnet2]
    
    D --> I[Clone qrefine into Phenix modules]
    I --> J{Need AQuaRef?}
    J -->|Yes| K[Run: update_phenix.sh aimnet2]
    J -->|No| L[Run: update_phenix.sh]
    
    F --> M[Installation Complete]
    G --> M
    H --> M
    K --> M
    L --> M
```

## Fully Automated Installation (Recommended)

The fully automated approach provides the simplest installation path, automatically detecting your Phenix installation type (installer or source build) and configuring all necessary components. This method copies the Q|R module files into your Phenix installation and updates the conda environment with required dependencies.

### Standard Installation

For a minimal installation without GPU acceleration, execute the following commands from the qrefine repository:

```bash
# Activate your Phenix environment
source path_to_phenix/phenix_env.sh

# Navigate to the qrefine repository
cd qrefine

# Run the automated installer
sh build_into_phenix.sh
```

The installer performs these operations automatically [build_into_phenix.sh](build_into_phenix.sh#L26-L85):
1. Detects Phenix installation type and location
2. Creates required directories (`modules/qrefine`, `build`)
3. Copies Q|R module files to Phenix
4. Updates Phenix's conda environment with base dependencies
5. Creates a symbolic link to `setpaths.sh` for easy activation

### Installation with AQuaRef (GPU Support)

For GPU-accelerated quantum refinement using AQuaRef (AIMNet2), include the `aimnet2` flag. This installs PyTorch and CUDA dependencies for GPU-accelerated calculations:

```bash
# For CUDA 12 (default, recommended for modern GPUs)
sh build_into_phenix.sh aimnet2

# For CUDA 11 (legacy GPU support)
sh build_into_phenix.sh aimnet2 cuda11
```

The AQuaRef components include [cuda12.yaml](config/cuda12.yaml#L1-L16):
- PyTorch with CUDA 12.1 support
- CUDA runtime and compiler components
- PyG (PyTorch Geometric) for graph neural networks
- Additional GPU-optimized dependencies

### Architecture Integration

The installation integrates Q|R into Phenix's modular architecture:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Phenix [Phenix Installation]
        direction TB
        P[Phenix Core]
        C[Conda Environment]
        M[modules/]
        B[build/]
        
        subgraph Qrefine [Q|R Integration]
            QR[modules/qrefine/]
            QC[qrefine_configure.log]
            SP[setpaths.sh]
        end
        
        subgraph Deps [Installed Dependencies]
            ASE[ASE 3.22.1]
            PM[PyMongo 4.8.0]
            XTB[xtb]
            TORCH[PyTorch + CUDA<br/>aimnet2 only]
        end
    end
    
    M --> QR
    B --> QC
    B --> SP
    C --> Deps
    
    style QR fill:#e1f5ff
    style Deps fill:#fff4e1
```

## Semi-Manual Installation (Developer Build)

The semi-manual approach provides greater flexibility for developers who need to update Q|R frequently, modify components during development, or add AQuaRef components at a later stage. This method gives you direct control over when updates are applied to your Phenix environment.

### Initial Setup

Clone the Q|R repository directly into your Phenix modules directory:

```bash
# Navigate to your Phenix installation directory
cd <phenix_installation>

# Clone qrefine into the modules directory
git clone https://github.com/qrefine/qrefine modules/qrefine
```

### Updating Phenix Environment

Use the `update_phenix.sh` script to update the Phenix conda environment with Q|R dependencies. This script supports multiple options for customization:

```bash
# Navigate to the qrefine module directory
cd modules/qrefine

# Standard installation (no GPU support)
sh config/update_phenix.sh

# Installation with AQuaRef (CUDA 12)
sh config/update_phenix.sh aimnet2

# Installation with AQuaRef (CUDA 11)
sh config/update_phenix.sh aimnet2 cuda11

# Skip confirmation prompt
sh config/update_phenix.sh aimnet2 -y
```

The update script [update_phenix.sh](config/update_phenix.sh#L14-L116):
1. Detects Phenix installation type (installer vs. source build)
2. Identifies the correct conda environment path
3. Detects system architecture (including Apple Silicon)
4. Configures Q|R module in the Phenix build system
5. Installs Python dependencies via pip
6. Optionally installs PyTorch and CUDA components for AQuaRef

### Dependency Installation

The script installs dependencies through two mechanisms. Base dependencies are installed via pip [phenix.txt](config/phenix.txt):

| Package | Version | Purpose |
|---------|---------|---------|
| ASE | 3.22.* | Atomic Simulation Environment for QM interface |
| PyMongo | 4.8.0 | Database connectivity for results storage |
| xtb | latest | Semi-empirical QM calculator |

For AQuaRef installations, GPU dependencies are managed through conda environment files [cuda12.yaml](config/cuda12.yaml#L1-L16) or [cuda11.yaml](config/cuda11.yaml#L1-L14):

| Component | CUDA 11 | CUDA 12 |
|-----------|---------|---------|
| PyTorch | `pytorch::pytorch=*=*cuda11*` | `pytorch::pytorch=*=*cuda12*` |
| PyTorch CUDA | 11.8 | 12.1 |
| CUDA Python | 11.8 | 12.1 |
| CUDA Toolkit | 11.8 | 12.1 + NVCC |
| BLAS | MKL | MKL |

> [!TIP]
> The AQuaRef installation via pip also installs the AIMNet2 calculation package directly from GitHub: `git+https://github.com/zubatyuk/aimnet2calc.git` [update_phenix.sh](config/update_phenix.sh#L110-L116)

## Platform-Specific Considerations

### Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3)

Apple Silicon (ARM64 architecture) requires special consideration. The installation script automatically detects ARM64 systems and skips AQuaRef installation due to compatibility issues [update_phenix.sh](config/update_phenix.sh#L52-L58):

```bash
if [[ $(uname -m) == "arm64" ]]; then
    ARM64=true
    echo "Found osx-arm64 (Apple Silicon) machine."
    echo "installation of aimnet2 will be skipped if requested"
    echo "Contact a developer to use aimnet2 on Apple Silicon"
    TORCH=false
fi
```

For Phenix installations on Apple Silicon, switch the BLAS implementation to Apple's Accelerate framework for optimal performance:

```bash
conda install -p <phenix_conda> libblas=*=*accelerate
```

> [!TIP]
> Clustering functionality is not recommended on Apple Silicon machines due to unreliable pair interactions. For CCTBX-only installations on Apple Silicon, use: `conda env create -n qrefine -f config/arm64-osx.yaml` [README.md](README.md#L40-L44)

### Permission Requirements

Depending on your Phenix installation location, you may need elevated permissions. If you encounter permission errors during installation:

```bash
# Use sudo if required
sudo sh build_into_phenix.sh aimnet2
```

## Post-Installation Configuration

### Activating Q|R in Phenix

After installation, activate the Q|R+Phenix environment in each new terminal session:

```bash
# Activate the configured environment
source <phenix_installation>/build/setpaths.sh
```

The automated installer creates a convenient symbolic link in the current directory for easy access [build_into_phenix.sh](build_into_phenix.sh#L82-L85):

```bash
ln -s $PHENIX/build/setpaths.sh .

# Future activation is simplified:
source ./setpaths.sh
```

**Recommendation**: Add the activation command to your `.bashrc` or `.zshrc` to automatically activate Q|R when starting terminal sessions:

```bash
echo "source <phenix_installation>/build/setpaths.sh" >> ~/.bashrc
```

### Verifying Installation

Test your Q|R installation by running the built-in test suite in an empty directory:

```bash
# Create and enter a test directory
mkdir tests
cd tests

# Run Q|R tests
qr.test
```

If any tests fail, please raise an issue on the [GitHub issue tracker](https://github.com/qrefine/qrefine/issues) [README.md](README.md#L52-L55).

## Installation Comparison

| Feature | Automated Installation | Semi-Manual Installation |
|---------|----------------------|--------------------------|
| **Complexity** | Simple, single command | Moderate, requires multiple steps |
| **Control** | Automatic configuration | Manual control over updates |
| **Use Case** | Production environments | Development environments |
| **Updates** | Re-run full script | Update selectively via update_phenix.sh |
| **AQuaRef** | Supported via flags | Supported via flags |
| **Developer Access** | Limited | Full access to source code |

## Troubleshooting

### Common Issues

**Phenix not detected**:
```bash
Error: "activate the phenix installation first!"
```
**Solution**: Ensure you've activated Phenix before running the installer:
```bash
source path_to_phenix/phenix_env.sh
```

**Conda permission errors**:
```bash
Error: Permission denied when updating conda environment
```
**Solution**: Use sudo or ensure you have write permissions to the Phenix directory.

**CUDA compatibility issues**:
```bash
Error: PyTorch CUDA version mismatch
```
**Solution**: Verify your GPU driver supports the requested CUDA version and install the appropriate variant (CUDA 11 or 12).

### Installation Logs

The installation process generates log files for troubleshooting:
- `qrefine_configure.log`: CCTBX configuration output [update_phenix.sh](config/update_phenix.sh#L88-L91)
- `qrefine_req.out`: Python dependency installation output [update_phenix.sh](config/update_phenix.sh#L96)
- `conda_aimnet2.out`: Conda environment updates for AQuaRef

Check these logs if installation encounters errors.

## Next Steps

After completing the Phenix installation, you can proceed to:

- **[CCTBX Installation](4-cctbx-installation)**: Alternative installation method for open-source CCTBX without Phenix
- **[Docker Setup](5-docker-setup)**: Containerized installation for reproducible environments
- **[Quick Start](2-quick-start)**: Begin using Q|R with example workflows
- **[Overview](1-overview)**: Learn more about Q|R's quantum refinement capabilities

For detailed information about AQuaRef performance optimization and configuration, refer to the [AQuaRef documentation](aimnet2.md) [README.md](README.md#L32-L35).


# CCTBX Installation



This guide provides a comprehensive walkthrough for installing Q|R using the open-source CCTBX (Computational Crystallography Toolbox) route. This installation method gives you full control over the environment and is ideal for developers or users who need access to the underlying framework. The installation process integrates Q|R directly into a CCTBX conda environment, enabling quantum-based refinement capabilities for biomolecular structures.

Sources: [cctbx.md](cctbx.md), [README.md](README.md)

## Prerequisites and Requirements

Before beginning the installation process, ensure your system meets the following requirements. The CCTBX installation path requires conda/mamba as the package manager and provides flexibility for different computing environments. For Apple Silicon users, special considerations are necessary due to platform-specific dependencies and BLAS library requirements.

The minimum system requirements include Python 3.9 or higher (with Q|R using 3.10 by default), a conda binary such as miniconda or mambaforge, and sufficient disk space for the complete CCTBX environment. For users planning to use GPU-accelerated features like AQuaRef with AIMNet2, a compatible NVIDIA GPU with appropriate CUDA drivers is required.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L20-L30), [environment.yaml](environment.yaml#L9-L10)

## Installation Architecture Overview

The CCTBX installation architecture follows a modular integration pattern where Q|R becomes a module within the CCTBX framework. This architecture enables seamless access to CCTBX's crystallographic tools while leveraging Q|R's quantum refinement capabilities. The installation process creates a structured environment where components are organized into specific directories within the Python site-packages.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Conda Environment Creation] --> B[CCTBX Installation]
    B --> C[Q|R Module Integration]
    C --> D[External Dependencies]
    D --> E[Build Configuration]
    E --> F[Runtime Setup]
    
    subgraph Environment
        A
        B
        C
    end
    
    subgraph Dependencies
        D
    end
    
    subgraph Runtime
        E
        F
    end
    
    style A fill:#e1f5ff
    style B fill:#e1f5ff
    style C fill:#fff4e1
    style D fill:#ffe1f5
    style E fill:#e1ffe1
    style F fill:#ffe1e1
```

This architectural flow demonstrates how the installation progresses from creating the conda environment through integrating Q|R as a module, handling external dependencies like reduce and probe, configuring the build system, and finally setting up runtime paths for execution.

Sources: [build_into_conda.sh](build_into_conda.sh#L15-L57), [README.md](README.md)

## Base Installation Process

The base installation follows a four-step process that establishes the complete CCTBX environment with Q|R integration. Each step builds upon the previous one, ensuring all components are properly configured and accessible.

**Step 1: Clone the Repository**

Begin by cloning the Q|R repository and entering its directory. This ensures you have the latest version of the codebase with all necessary configuration files and installation scripts.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/qrefine/qrefine.git qrefine && cd qrefine
```

Sources: [cctbx.md](cctbx.md#L2-L6)

**Step 2: Create Conda Environment**

The `environment.yaml` file defines all necessary dependencies including CCTBX nightly builds, essential Python packages like numpy and networkx, cheminformatics tools like rdkit, and quantum chemistry packages like MOPAC and xTB. Execute the following commands to create and activate the qrefine environment:

```bash
conda env create -n qrefine -f environment.yaml
conda activate qrefine
```

This step creates a complete environment with Python 3.10, CCTBX libraries, and all supporting packages. The environment activation command must be run in every new shell session where you intend to use Q|R.

Sources: [cctbx.md](cctbx.md#L8-L17), [environment.yaml](environment.yaml)

**Step 3: Integrate Q|R into CCTBX**

The integration process is automated through the `build_into_conda.sh` script, which performs several critical operations. First, it identifies the Python site-packages directory and copies the Q|R module into a structured modules hierarchy. The script then downloads and configures external dependencies including reduce (for hydrogen atom placement), creates the build directory structure, and establishes symbolic links to executable files. Finally, it runs `libtbx.configure` to register Q|R, reduce, and probe with the CCTBX system, and rebuilds necessary rotamer and backbone dihedral angle caches.

```bash
bash ./build_into_conda.sh
```

Sources: [build_into_conda.sh](build_into_conda.sh#L12-L57)

**Step 4: Configure Runtime Paths**

The installation script concludes by outputting a `source` command that sets up the required runtime paths. This command must be executed in every new shell session to ensure all CCTBX and Q|R executables and libraries are accessible. The command typically appears as:

```bash
source <path>/setpaths.sh
```

For convenience, this command can be added to your `.bashrc` or equivalent shell configuration file to automate the setup for new sessions.

Sources: [cctbx.md](cctbx.md#L24-L26), [build_into_conda.sh](build_into_conda.sh#L53-L56)

## Platform-Specific Configurations

Different computing platforms require specific configuration adjustments to ensure optimal performance and compatibility. The Q|R project provides specialized configuration files for various scenarios.

### Standard Linux Installation

The standard Linux installation uses `environment.yaml` with the default BLAS configuration. This configuration is suitable for most x86-64 systems and provides access to all core features including CUDA support through pytorch integration.

Sources: [environment.yaml](environment.yaml), [config/cuda12.yaml](config/cuda12.yaml)

### Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3) Installation

Apple Silicon systems require special handling due to architecture differences and BLAS library compatibility. Use the specialized configuration file for arm64-osx systems:

```bash
conda env create -n qrefine -f config/arm64-osx.yaml
conda activate qrefine
```

The arm64-osx configuration switches to Apple's accelerate BLAS implementation and uses a specific CCTBX version (2024.12) rather than the nightly builds. **Important limitation**: Clustering functionality is unreliable on Apple Silicon machines due to unknown issues with pair interaction calculations. The configuration also omits xtb and numba packages which may have compatibility issues on this platform.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L37-L44), [config/arm64-osx.yaml](config/arm64-osx.yaml)

> [!TIP]
> Apple Silicon users experiencing stability issues with clustering should consider using alternative fragmentation strategies or running the workload on x86-64 hardware for production calculations.

### CUDA and GPU Acceleration

For GPU-accelerated calculations using AQuaRef with AIMNet2, additional CUDA dependencies are required. The project provides configuration files for both CUDA 11.8 and CUDA 12.1 versions. After the base installation, update the environment with CUDA support:

```bash
conda env update -f config/cuda12.yaml  # or cuda11.yaml
```

These configurations add PyTorch with CUDA support, CUDA Python bindings, numba for just-in-time compilation, and PyTorch Geometric for graph neural network operations. The choice between CUDA versions depends on your GPU hardware and driver compatibility.

Sources: [config/cuda11.yaml](config/cuda11.yaml), [config/cuda12.yaml](config/cuda12.yaml)

## AQuaRef and AIMNet2 Integration

AQuaRef provides AI-powered quantum refinement capabilities using the AIMNet2 neural network potential. This advanced feature requires additional installation steps beyond the base CCTBX setup. AIMNet2 enables significantly faster calculations compared to traditional quantum chemistry methods while maintaining high accuracy.

### Installation Steps

After completing the base CCTBX installation, install the AIMNet2 calculator package:

```bash
conda env update -f config/aimnet2.yaml
qrefine.python -m pip install git+https://github.com/zubatyuk/aimnet2calc.git
```

The `config/aimnet2.yaml` file adds PyTorch with CUDA support, CUDA Python libraries, numba, PyTorch Geometric, and other dependencies required for neural network potentials. The pip command installs the AIMNet2 calculator interface that connects Q|R to the neural network model.

Sources: [aimnet2.md](aimnet2.md#L1-L14), [config/aimnet2.yaml](config/aimnet2.yaml)

### Performance Optimization

For optimal performance with CUDA-accelerated calculations, set the following environment variable:

```bash
export NUMBA_CUDA_USE_NVIDIA_BINDING=1
```

Add this to your `.bashrc` file to make it persistent across sessions. To verify that CUDA components are working correctly, run the following test commands:

```bash
qrefine.python -c "import numba.cuda; print(numba.cuda.is_available())"
qrefine.python -c "import torch; print(torch.cuda.is_available())"
```

Both commands should return `True` indicating that CUDA is properly detected and accessible.

Sources: [aimnet2.md](aimnet2.md#L30-L55)

## Configuration Comparison

The following table summarizes the different configuration options available for CCTBX installation:

| Configuration File | Target Platform | CCTBX Version | BLAS Library | CUDA Support | Special Features |
|-------------------|-----------------|--------------|--------------|--------------|------------------|
| environment.yaml | Standard Linux | Nightly build | Default (MKL) | PyTorch CUDA | Full feature set |
| config/arm64-osx.yaml | Apple Silicon | 2024.12 | Apple Accelerate | None | Optimized for M1/M2/M3 |
| config/cuda11.yaml | Linux + NVIDIA | Nightly build | MKL | CUDA 11.8 | Older GPU support |
| config/cuda12.yaml | Linux + NVIDIA | Nightly build | MKL | CUDA 12.1 | Latest GPU support |
| config/aimnet2.yaml | Linux + NVIDIA | Nightly build | MKL | Flexible | Neural network potentials |

Sources: [environment.yaml](environment.yaml), [config/arm64-osx.yaml](config/arm64-osx.yaml), [config/cuda11.yaml](config/cuda11.yaml), [config/cuda12.yaml](config/cuda12.yaml), [config/aimnet2.yaml](config/aimnet2.yaml)

## Directory Structure After Installation

After successful installation, Q|R integrates into the CCTBX environment with the following directory structure within your Python site-packages:

```
<site-packages>/
├── build/
│   ├── setpaths.sh                    # Runtime configuration script
│   ├── probe/exe/                      # Probe executable symlink
│   └── reduce/exe/                     # Reduce executable symlink
├── modules/
│   └── qrefine/                        # Complete Q|R source code
│       ├── command_line/               # Command-line interfaces
│       ├── plugin/ase/                 # QM calculator wrappers
│       ├── config/                     # Configuration files
│       ├── qr.py                       # Main refinement module
│       └── ...
├── iotbx/pdb/
│   └── hybrid_36_c.c                   # Reduce hybrid-36 encoding
└── ...
```

The build directory contains the runtime configuration and symbolic links to external executables. The modules/qrefine directory holds the complete Q|R codebase, enabling seamless integration with CCTBX tools.

Sources: [build_into_conda.sh](build_into_conda.sh#L27-L56), [command_line/qr.py](command_line/qr.py), [plugin/ase/README.md](plugin/ase/README.md)

## Verification and Testing

After installation, verify that Q|R is properly configured by running the built-in test suite. Tests must be executed in an empty directory to avoid conflicts with existing files:

```bash
mkdir tests
cd tests
qr.test
```

The test suite covers core functionality including fragmentation, restraint generation, quantum calculations, and refinement processes. If any tests fail, please report the issue through the [GitHub issue tracker](https://github.com/qrefine/qrefine/issues) with details about your system configuration and the specific test failures.

For a quick verification of available command-line options and default values, use:

```bash
qr.refine --show-defaults
```

This displays all configurable parameters and their default settings, providing insight into the available refinement options.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L48-L57), [README.md](README.md#L63-L69)

## Project Repository Structure

The following diagram illustrates the key directories in the Q|R repository that are relevant to CCTBX installation:

```mermaid
graph TD
    Root[qrefine/] --> Config[config/]
    Root --> Plugin[plugin/]
    Root --> Command[command_line/]
    Root --> Scripts[Installation Scripts]
    Root --> Tests[tests/]
    
    Config --> BaseYAML[environment.yaml]
    Config --> Arm64[arm64-osx.yaml]
    Config --> CUDA11[cuda11.yaml]
    Config --> CUDA12[cuda12.yaml]
    Config --> AIMNET[aimnet2.yaml]
    
    Plugin --> ASE[ase/]
    ASE --> Calculators[QM Calculator Wrappers]
    
    Command --> QR[qr.py - CLI Interface]
    
    Scripts --> BuildConda[build_into_conda.sh]
    Scripts --> BuildPhenix[build_into_phenix.sh]
    
    Tests --> Unit[unit/ - Unit Tests]
    Tests --> Regression[regression/ - Regression Tests]
    Tests --> Acceptance[acceptance/ - Acceptance Tests]
    
    style Config fill:#e1f5ff
    style Plugin fill:#fff4e1

    style Tests fill:#ffe1f5
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md), [cctbx.md](cctbx.md), [build_into_conda.sh](build_into_conda.sh)

## Docker Alternative

For users who prefer containerized environments, a Docker image is available that encapsulates the complete CCTBX + Q|R setup with CUDA12 support. The Dockerfile demonstrates the complete installation process in a reproducible format:

```bash
docker pull qrefine/cctbx-qr
```

The Docker image includes the base CCTBX environment, CUDA12 dependencies, complete Q|R integration, and the AIMNet2 calculator. This approach eliminates environment configuration issues and provides consistency across different host systems.

Sources: [Dockerfile](Dockerfile#L1-L37), [README.md](README.md#L3-L6)

## Alternative Installation Routes

While this guide focuses on the CCTBX installation route, alternative installation methods are available depending on your use case. For users with existing Phenix installations, the [Phenix Installation](3-phenix-installation) route provides tighter integration with the Phenix refinement suite and may be more suitable for crystallography workflows. The Docker setup offers another containerization option with pre-configured environments.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L19-L22), [phenix.md](phenix.md)

These resources will help you progress from installation to productive use of Q|R for quantum-based refinement of biomolecular structures.


# Docker Setup



The Docker setup for qrefine provides a **complete, pre-configured environment** that eliminates the complexity of manual installation. This approach delivers a reproducible computational environment with all dependencies—including CCTBX, quantum chemistry calculators, and CUDA support—pre-installed and ready to use. The Docker images are particularly valuable for researchers who need immediate access to quantum refinement capabilities without navigating complex dependency resolution.

![Docker Hub Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/dockerhub-images-important.svg?logo=Docker)

## Docker Image Architecture

The qrefine Docker implementation follows a **layered build strategy** designed around conda-forge's mambaforge as the base layer. This architecture provides a clean separation between the base conda environment, CUDA/PyTorch dependencies, and qrefine-specific installation. The build process systematically creates a complete scientific computing stack with optimized linear algebra libraries (MKL) and GPU acceleration capabilities.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A[Base: mambaforge/latest] --> B[Install qrefine env<br/>environment.yaml]
    B --> C[Add CUDA 12 dependencies<br/>config/cuda12.yaml]
    C --> D[Build qrefine<br/>build_into_conda.sh]
    D --> E[Install AIMNet2 calculator<br/>pip install]
    E --> F[Final image<br/>cctbx-cuda env ready]
    
    style A fill:#e1f5e1
    style B fill:#fff4e1
    style C fill:#ffe1f5
    style D fill:#e1f0ff
    style E fill:#f5e1ff
    style F fill:#e1ffe1
```

The Docker image creation involves several critical stages that transform the base conda distribution into a fully functional quantum refinement environment. Each layer builds upon the previous one, starting with CCTBX essentials and extending through CUDA integration to the final qrefine module installation.

Sources: [Dockerfile](Dockerfile#L1-L37), [environment.yaml](environment.yaml#L1-L22), [config/cuda12.yaml](config/cuda12.yaml#L1-L16)

## Available Docker Images

qrefine provides pre-built Docker images through Docker Hub, with support for different CUDA versions to match your hardware environment. The images are optimized for NVIDIA GPU acceleration but can also run in CPU-only mode for testing or smaller systems.

| Image Variant | CUDA Version | Base Image | PyTorch Backend | Best For |
|--------------|--------------|------------|----------------|----------|
| `qrefine/cctbx-qr:latest` | 12.1 | mambaforge | CUDA 12.1 | Modern NVIDIA GPUs (RTX 30xx/40xx) |
| `qrefine/cctbx-qr:cuda11` | 11.8 | mambaforge | CUDA 11.8 | Legacy NVIDIA GPUs |
| Custom builds | 11.8 or 12.1 | mambaforge | Configurable | Specific CUDA requirements |

The **default image** includes CUDA 12.1 support, which provides access to the latest GPU-accelerated quantum chemistry calculators including AIMNet2 through PyTorch. For systems with older GPU hardware that doesn't support CUDA 12, the CUDA 11.8 variant ensures compatibility while maintaining full functionality.

Sources: [Dockerfile](Dockerfile#L7-L8), [config/cuda12.yaml](config/cuda12.yaml#L4-L6), [config/cuda11.yaml](config/cuda11.yaml#L4-L6)

## Build Process Details

The Docker build process orchestrates the installation of qrefine through a sequence of carefully controlled steps. The Dockerfile executes `build_into_conda.sh` which handles the complex CCTBX module configuration, including setting up the necessary build directories, creating symbolic links for external tools (probe, reduce), and running the libtbx configure process. This ensures that qrefine is properly integrated into the CCTBX ecosystem.

> [!TIP]
> The build script creates a special build directory structure (`$PACKAGES/build/`) that contains symlinks to the probe and reduce executables. This is critical for the libtbx configure step to locate these dependencies correctly. The final environment must be activated using `source setpaths.sh` from this build directory to properly configure the CCTBX runtime environment.

The installation process also downloads and compiles the reduce tool from GitHub, patching the CCTBX source with the updated `hybrid_36_c.c` file for improved handling of residue numbering. This level of integration ensures that all tools work seamlessly together within the Docker environment.

Sources: [build_into_conda.sh](build_into_conda.sh#L1-L57), [Dockerfile](Dockerfile#L19-L20)

## Environment Configuration

The Docker image configures several critical environment variables to optimize performance and ensure proper execution of quantum refinement calculations. These settings control OpenMP thread behavior, Python buffering, and CUDA integration.

| Environment Variable | Value | Purpose |
|---------------------|-------|---------|
| `OMP_MAX_ACTIVE_LEVELS` | 1 | Prevents nested parallelism issues |
| `OMP_STACKSIZE` | 4G | Allocates sufficient stack for large calculations |
| `PYTHONUNBUFFERED` | true | Immediate output streaming |
| `GFORTRAN_UNBUFFERED_ALL` | 1 | Ensures Fortran output is not buffered |
| `NUMBA_CUDA_USE_NVIDIA_BINDING` | 1 | Enables proper CUDA Numba integration |
| `PATH` | Extended | Includes conda env and build tools |

The conda environment is named `cctbx-cuda` and is automatically activated through the bashrc configuration. This environment contains the complete scientific stack including numpy, networkx, rdkit, ASE, and both MOPAC and xtb calculators pre-installed and configured.

Sources: [Dockerfile](Dockerfile#L25-L33), [environment.yaml](environment.yaml#L10-L20)

## Running qrefine in Docker

### Basic Usage

Running qrefine in Docker requires mounting your data directories into the container to access input files and store results. The default working directory is `/mnt`, making it straightforward to map your data directory to this location.

```bash
# Pull the latest image
docker pull qrefine/cctbx-qr:latest

# Run qrefine with mounted data directory
docker run --gpus all -it \
  -v /path/to/your/data:/mnt \
  qrefine/cctbx-qr:latest \
  qr.refine your_protein.pdb your_map.mtz mode=refine engine=mopac
```

The `--gpus all` flag is essential for GPU-accelerated calculations. For CPU-only operation or testing, omit this flag to run in container mode without GPU access.

### Advanced GPU Configuration

For systems with multiple GPUs or specific GPU requirements, you can control GPU access more precisely:

```bash
# Use specific GPU device
docker run --gpus '"device=0"' -it \
  -v /path/to/your/data:/mnt \
  qrefine/cctbx-qr:latest \
  qr.refine your_protein.pdb your_map.mtz engine=aimnet2

# Limit GPU memory usage
docker run --gpus all -e CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 -it \
  -v /path/to/your/data:/mnt \
  qrefine/cctbx-qr:latest \
  qr.refine your_protein.pdb your_map.mtz engine=xtb
```

### Interactive Development

For interactive development and testing, you can access a shell within the container:

```bash
docker run --gpus all -it \
  -v /path/to/your/data:/mnt \
  qrefine/cctbx-qr:latest \
  /bin/bash

# Inside container, run qrefine commands
conda activate cctbx-cuda
qr.refine --show-defaults
```

Sources: [Dockerfile](Dockerfile#L35-L36), [README.md](README.md#L68-L77)

## Calculator Support

The Docker image comes with **multiple quantum chemistry calculators** pre-configured and ready to use. The selection of calculator depends on your specific requirements for accuracy, speed, and system size.

| Calculator | Pre-installed | GPU Accelerated | Use Case |
|------------|---------------|------------------|----------|
| MOPAC | ✓ | ✗ | Fast semi-empirical, large systems |
| xTB | ✓ | ✗ | Tight-binding, good accuracy/speed balance |
| AIMNet2 | ✓ | ✓ | Machine learning, very fast for large proteins |
| Gaussian | Additional install | ✗ | High accuracy DFT/ab initio |
| ORCA | Additional install | ✗ | Advanced quantum chemistry methods |

> [!TIP]
> AIMNet2 is particularly effective in the Docker environment because it leverages the pre-installed PyTorch CUDA stack. The installation command `qrefine.python -m pip install git+https://github.com/zubatyuk/aimnet2calc.git` is executed during the Docker build, ensuring that the neural network potentials are available without additional configuration.

For calculators not pre-installed (like Gaussian or ORCA), you can install them within the Docker container or mount external installations into the container. The ASE plugin architecture in `/plugin/ase/` provides interfaces for all supported calculators.

Sources: [Dockerfile](Dockerfile#L23), [environment.yaml](environment.yaml#L18-L19), [plugin/ase](plugin/ase/)

## Building Custom Images

While pre-built images are available, you may need to build custom images for specific requirements, such as different CUDA versions or additional system packages. The build process uses the repository's Dockerfile and configuration files.

```bash
# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/qrefine/qrefine.git
cd qrefine

# Build with CUDA 12 (default)
docker build -t my-qrefine:latest .

# Build with modified CUDA version
# Edit Dockerfile to use config/cuda11.yaml instead
docker build -t my-qrefine:cuda11 .
```

The build process requires approximately **2-4 GB of disk space** for the final image and may take 15-30 minutes depending on your internet connection speed (for downloading conda packages) and CPU performance (for compilation steps).

# Quantum Refinement Concepts



Quantum refinement represents a fundamental paradigm shift in macromolecular structure determination, replacing traditional parameterized library-based restraints with quantum chemical restraints derived from first principles. This approach offers two critical advantages: increased accuracy for non-standard molecules (novel cofactors, drug molecules) and the ability to generate chemically meaningful restraints for systems lacking comprehensive library parameters. The implementation addresses computational scaling challenges through a sophisticated fragmentation-based divide-and-conquer strategy.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L35), [refine.py](refine.py#L1-L20)

## Core Architecture

The quantum refinement system implements a modular architecture that integrates quantum mechanical calculations with crystallographic refinement machinery. The system orchestrates multiple specialized components to achieve simultaneous optimization against experimental data and quantum chemical potentials.

The architectural foundation rests on five primary components that collaborate during refinement cycles:

- **fmodel**: Crystallographic information container managing structure factors, electron density maps, and the x-ray structure model
- **calculator**: Composite object computing total energy and gradients by combining data terms with restraint terms
- **restraints_manager**: Selects between quantum mechanical (QM) or classical (CCTBX) restraint sources for energy and gradient calculations
- **geometry_restraints_manager**: Analyzes geometric quality through bond and angle RMSD metrics
- **weights**: Adaptive scale factors balancing experimental data against restraint contributions

Sources: [refine.py](refine.py#L5-L19), [driver.py](driver.py#L1-L30)

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph Input["Input Layer"]
        PDB[PDB Model]
        MTZ[Experimental Data]
    end
    
    subgraph Core["Core Refinement Engine"]
        fmodel[fmodel<br/>Crystallographic Info]
        calc[calculator<br/>Energy & Gradients]
        rm[restraints_manager<br/>QM or CCTBX]
        grm[geometry_manager<br/>RMSD Analysis]
        weights[adaptive_weights<br/>Data/Restraint Balance]
    end
    
    subgraph Output["Output Layer"]
        mon[monitor<br/>Results Tracking]
        PDB_out[Refined PDB]
        Logs[Refinement Logs]
    end
    
    PDB --> fmodel
    MTZ --> fmodel
    fmodel --> calc
    rm --> calc
    weights --> calc
    calc --> mon
    grm --> mon
    mon --> PDB_out
    mon --> Logs
```

The calculator module serves as the central integration point, implementing an adaptive weight factor calculator that dynamically adjusts restraint influence based on geometric quality. When bond RMSD exceeds thresholds, the system scales restraint weights upward to maintain geometric integrity, while high-quality geometry triggers weight reduction to allow greater influence from experimental data.

Sources: [calculator.py](calculator.py#L1-L10), [calculator.py](calculator.py#L26-L62)

## Restraint Systems

Quantum refinement provides two fundamentally different restraint sources that can be applied selectively or complementarily across molecular regions.

**CCTBX Classical Restraints**: Standard crystallographic restraints derived from comprehensive parameter libraries containing idealized bond lengths, angles, and torsions. These restraints are computationally efficient but may lack accuracy for novel chemical entities or unusual bonding patterns. The `from_cctbx` class wraps the standard CCTBX restraints manager, providing seamless integration with legacy refinement workflows.

Sources: [restraints.py](restraints.py#L389-L433)

**Quantum Mechanical Restraints**: First-principles restraints computed directly from quantum chemical calculations on molecular fragments. The `from_qm` class interfaces with various QM engines to compute electronic structure energies and analytic gradients, providing chemically rigorous force information. This approach eliminates dependence on parameter libraries and can handle arbitrary chemical systems with appropriate quantum methods.

The QM restraints system supports multiple computational methods and basis sets:
- Semi-empirical methods (PM7, AM1) for rapid evaluation
- Density functional theory with various functionals
- Hartree-Fock with flexible basis set selection
- Machine learning potentials (AIMNet2) for acceleration

Sources: [restraints.py](restraints.py#L434-L479), [refine.py](refine.py#L240-L275)

> [!TIP]
> The choice between CCTBX and QM restraints can be made atom-wise through selection mechanisms, allowing hybrid approaches where novel regions use quantum restraints while well-characterized regions use efficient classical restraints.

| Restraint Type | Advantages | Limitations | Computational Cost |
|----------------|------------|-------------|-------------------|
| CCTBX Classical | Fast, well-tested, extensive libraries | Limited accuracy for novel chemistries | Very Low |
| QM Semi-empirical | Good accuracy for diverse chemistry | Parameter-specific approximations | Low-Medium |
| QM DFT/HF | First-principles accuracy | High computational demand | High |
| ML Potentials | Near-DFT accuracy, fast | Training set dependence, transferability | Low |

## Weight Factor Optimization

A critical innovation in quantum refinement is the adaptive weight factor calculation that automatically balances experimental data against restraint contributions. The system computes initial weights by comparing gradient magnitudes from crystallographic data and restraint sources, then iteratively adjusts based on geometric quality metrics.

The weight optimization cycle follows a disciplined search pattern:
1. Compute initial data weight from gradient norm ratios
2. Execute refinement with current weights
3. Evaluate geometry quality (bond/angle RMSD)
4. If geometry exceeds quality thresholds, increase restraint weight
5. If geometry is within quality bounds, decrease restraint weight
6. Terminate when weight adjustment direction reverses, indicating optimal balance

This adaptive approach eliminates the need for manual weight tuning while ensuring that refinement respects both experimental data and chemical reality. The gradient-based weight calculation filters outliers (large gradient components) to avoid skewing the balance from problematic atoms.

Sources: [calculator.py](calculator.py#L26-L62), [driver.py](driver.py#L330-L380)

## Fragmentation Strategy

To achieve quantum refinement of macromolecular systems, Q|R implements a sophisticated fragmentation strategy that divides large systems into computationally tractable quantum chemical regions. The `fragments` class manages this process, creating clusters that expand beyond the core fragment to include environmental effects through embedding atoms.

Key fragmentation parameters control the computational scale:
- **maxnum_residues_in_cluster**: Limits cluster size to maintain QM tractability
- **select_within_radius**: Defines the spatial extent of cluster expansion (default 10 Å)
- **bcc_threshold**: Determines buffer atom selection criteria
- **charge_embedding**: Whether to include electrostatic embedding from distant atoms
- **two_buffers**: Controls whether to use dual buffer layers for environmental capture

The fragmentation process identifies covalent fragments, generates spatially-expanded clusters for QM evaluation, and coordinates the distribution of QM calculations across fragments. For systems with substantial conformational changes during refinement, dynamic re-clustering can be triggered based on RMSD thresholds.

Sources: [fragment.py](fragment.py#L43-L113), [driver.py](driver.py#L128-L150)

## Refinement Optimization Engine

The refinement process employs multiple optimization algorithms tailored to different refinement scenarios. The primary engine uses the L-BFGS (Limited-memory Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno) quasi-Newton method, which provides efficient convergence for large-scale optimization problems by approximating the Hessian matrix from gradient history.

The minimization process operates through the `minimizer` class, which:
- Coordinates L-BFGS iteration with configurable line search options
- Monitors function and gradient evaluations for convergence detection
- Tracks geometric quality through RMSD calculations
- Supports gradient-only mode for scenarios where line search is computationally expensive
- Implements exception handling to manage numerical challenges in optimization

Alternative optimization paths include:
- **Pre-conjugate gradient minimization**: Initial steepest descent steps before transitioning to conjugate gradient methods
- **ASE LBFGS interface**: Integration with Atomic Simulation Environment optimization tools
- **Real-space refinement**: Direct map-based optimization using real-space correlation targets

The refinement cycles execute macro-level iterations where weights may be adjusted between minimization runs, allowing the system to find the optimal balance between data and restraints.

Sources: [driver.py](driver.py#L25-L98), [driver.py](driver.py#L100-L200)

## Results Monitoring and Convergence

The `results.manager` class provides comprehensive tracking of refinement progress through multiple metrics that characterize model quality. This monitoring system captures:

- **Crystallographic metrics**: R-work and R-free values measuring agreement with experimental data
- **Geometric metrics**: Bond and angle RMSDs quantifying stereochemical quality
- **Coordinate shifts**: Atomic displacement statistics comparing initial, previous, and current coordinates
- **Convergence tracking**: Iteration history showing optimization progress

Convergence criteria balance multiple objectives:
- Gradient norms approaching zero (mathematical stationarity)
- R-factor stabilization (data fit saturation)
- Geometry within acceptable bounds (chemical reasonableness)
- Coordinate shifts diminishing (model stability)

The system writes checkpoint files (`.rst.pickle`) enabling restart capabilities and provides final PDB output files with complete refinement annotations.

Sources: [results.py](results.py#L1-L50), [driver.py](driver.py#L380-L400)

> [!TIP]
> The monitoring system computes mean shifts between refinement stages, enabling early detection of oscillatory behavior that may indicate weight factor instability or problematic local minima.

## Hybrid Approaches and Alternative Conformations

Quantum refinement supports sophisticated handling of structural complexity through specialized restraint managers for systems with alternative conformations.

The `from_altlocs` and `from_altlocs2` classes provide mechanisms for:
- **Alternative conformation handling**: Managing multiple conformational states while maintaining proper restraint application
- **Selective refinement**: Applying quantum restraints to specific conformations while using classical restraints elsewhere
- **Gradient combination**: Combining contributions from multiple conformational states with appropriate statistical weighting

These capabilities enable refinement of dynamic systems where atoms occupy multiple discrete positions, ensuring that quantum chemical restraints properly account for conformational heterogeneity. The system can subtract or combine gradients from alternate states based on user-specified methods.

Sources: [restraints.py](restraints.py#L257-L366)

## Next Steps

To apply quantum refinement concepts practically, continue to [Understanding Fragmentation](7-understanding-fragmentation) to learn how the fragmentation strategy is implemented and configured for specific systems. For details on available quantum chemical engines, proceed to [Supported QM Engines Overview](11-supported-qm-engines-overview).

# Understanding Fragmentation



Fragmentation is a fundamental strategy that enables quantum mechanical refinement of macromolecular structures by dividing complex systems into computationally tractable pieces. This approach balances quantum mechanical accuracy with practical computational efficiency, allowing QM refinement of proteins and nucleic acids that would otherwise be prohibitively expensive to calculate as whole systems. The fragmentation system orchestrates a sophisticated workflow from initial molecular decomposition through to quantum-ready fragments with proper boundary conditions and electrostatic embedding.

## The Fragmentation Architecture

The fragmentation architecture implements a hierarchical decomposition strategy that transforms a complete macromolecular system into a collection of quantum-mechanically tractable fragments. At its core, the system operates through three distinct but interconnected phases: clustering creates molecular groupings based on interaction networks, expansion builds buffer regions around each cluster, and electrostatic embedding establishes the QM/MM boundary conditions. This multi-layered approach ensures that each quantum calculation operates on a chemically meaningful subset while maintaining the essential intermolecular interactions present in the full system.

The architecture is built around the `fragments` class in [fragment.py](fragment.py#L43-L120), which serves as the central coordinator for the entire decomposition process. This class manages the workflow from initial hierarchy parsing through fragment generation, handling complex scenarios like alternative conformations, periodic boundary conditions, and charge embedding. The design deliberately separates concerns: clustering algorithms identify coherent molecular groups, super-cell expansion handles spatial boundaries, and completion modules establish proper capping groups for fragment termini.

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[PDB Hierarchy + Crystal Symmetry] --> B[Super Cell Expansion]
    B --> C[Interaction Network Generation]
    C --> D[Graph Clustering Algorithm]
    D --> E[Cluster Identification]
    E --> F[Buffer Region Generation]
    F --> G[Fragment Assembly]
    G --> H[Alternative Conformation Handling]
    H --> I[Charge Completion & Capping]
    I --> J[QM-Ready Fragments]
    
    K[Parameters] --> D
    L[Engine Configuration] --> I
    M[Altloc Method] --> H
```

## Clustering Phase: Creating Molecular Groups

The clustering phase represents the foundation of the fragmentation strategy, where the system decomposes into coherent molecular groups based on interaction networks. This process constructs a graph where vertices represent individual residues and edges encode pairwise interactions, then applies community detection algorithms to identify natural molecular neighborhoods. The default clustering algorithm is betweenness centrality clustering, though Girvan-Newman clustering remains available as an alternative implementation.

Betweenness centrality clustering, implemented in the `betweenness_centrality_clustering` class ([clustering.py#L83-L133](clustering.py#L83-L133)), progressively removes edges with high betweenness centrality values to reveal natural community structures. The algorithm builds an undirected graph from interaction pairs ([clustering.py#L121-L133](clustering.py#L121-L133)), then iteratively applies edge removal at decreasing threshold values until no cluster exceeds the `maxnum_residues_in_cluster` parameter ([clustering.py#L94-L104](clustering.py#L94-L104)). This adaptive threshold approach ensures clusters respect both interaction density and size constraints.

> [!TIP]
> The interaction network intentionally includes backbone connections from [`fragment_utils.get_backbone_connections()`](utils/fragment_utils.py#L2-L17), ensuring polypeptide chains remain coherent even when intra-chain interactions are weak. This prevents unnatural fragmentation that would break peptide bonds in proteins or phosphate backbones in nucleic acids.

The clustering process automatically handles special structural cases. For proteins, backbone connections between consecutive amino acids are explicitly added to preserve peptide bond continuity ([fragment.py#L122-L124](fragment.py#L122-L124)). The system identifies amino acids through the presence of N, CA, C, and O atoms ([utils/fragment_utils.py#L20-L34](utils/fragment_utils.py#L20-L34)), ensuring backbone tracking applies specifically to polypeptide rather than general molecular connections.

| **Clustering Parameter** | **Default** | **Purpose** | **Impact on QM Calculations** |
|-------------------------|-------------|-------------|-------------------------------|
| `maxnum_residues_in_cluster` | 20 | Maximum cluster size | Direct QM cost scaling, larger clusters are more expensive |
| `bcc_threshold` | 9 | Initial betweenness centrality cutoff | Controls cluster granularity, higher values create fewer, larger clusters |
| `clustering_method` | betweenness_centrality | Algorithm selection | Determines interaction sensitivity and cluster characteristics |

## Fragment Generation: From Clusters to QM Regions

Once clustering identifies molecular neighborhoods, the fragment generation phase expands each cluster into a quantum-mechanically complete region. This expansion creates buffer regions of surrounding molecules that provide boundary conditions for the QM calculation while avoiding explicit quantum treatment of distant portions of the system. The `get_fragments()` method in the fragments class ([fragment.py#L130-L290](fragment.py#L130-L290)) orchestrates this complex transformation, handling atomic indexing, spatial selection, and hierarchical organization across multiple conformational states.

The fragment generation process operates on an expanded coordinate system that includes periodic boundary conditions. The `_expand()` method ([fragment.py#L98-L107](fragment.py#L98-L107)) creates a super-cell expansion using the [`super_cell.expand`](super_cell.py#L20-L91) class, which generates symmetry-related molecules within a specified radius (`select_within_radius`, default 10.0 Å). This expansion ensures that fragments near unit cell boundaries have access to relevant neighboring molecules that would otherwise be excluded by simple distance calculations.

Each fragment consists of two distinct components: the cluster itself and a surrounding buffer region. The cluster contains the core molecules identified during the clustering phase, while the buffer includes additional molecules within interaction range. This distinction is crucial because cluster atoms typically receive QM treatment with full weighting, whereas buffer atoms may receive different treatment depending on the embedding strategy. The system tracks these regions separately through `cluster_atoms` and `fragment_super_atoms` attributes ([fragment.py#L166-L170](fragment.py#L166-L170)).

> [!TIP]
> Optional double buffering (`two_buffers=True`) creates an additional expansion layer, useful when fragments require even larger boundary regions to capture long-range electrostatic effects or when studying charge transfer phenomena that extend beyond typical interaction distances.

The fragment generation pipeline demonstrates sophisticated handling of alternative conformations. When alternative locations (altlocs) are present, the system generates separate hierarchy selections for each conformational state ([fragment.py#L138-L152](fragment.py#L138-L152)), allowing independent fragment definitions for structural variants. This prevents mixing incompatible conformations in single QM calculations while maintaining proper accounting of occupancies across the full ensemble.

## Alternative Conformation Strategies

Alternative conformations represent a significant challenge in fragmentation because atoms at the same position may exist in multiple mutually exclusive states. The fragmentation system provides two sophisticated strategies for handling these situations: the "subtract" method and the "average" method, selectable through the `altloc_method` parameter. Both approaches address the fundamental problem that atoms with alternative conformations cannot simultaneously participate in QM calculations with incompatible neighbors.

The "subtract" strategy implements a clean separation approach where each alternative conformation receives independent fragment definitions. When fragments differ between conformations, the system subtracts overlapping contributions to prevent double-counting ([fragment.py#L195-L213](fragment.py#L195-L213)).
